slides.title: Laws that shape frontend code
slides.summary: Privacy, accessibility and payment rules all have concrete requirements for the UI.
body: Compliance isn't only a legal team's job. Many requirements land directly in frontend code: what you store, what you track, and how you ask for consent.
<mark>Collect the least personal data you need, and don't load trackers before the user agrees.</mark>

body.note: This is an engineering overview, not legal advice. Check what applies to your product and users with your legal team.

cells.text: Consent, data minimisation, right to delete and export
Ask before non-essential cookies and trackers
“Do not sell or share” link, honour Global Privacy Control
Use hosted payment fields; control scripts on payment pages
No PHI in URLs, logs or analytics
Accessible UI is a legal requirement in many markets

slides.title: Privacy by design in the UI
slides.summary: Consent before tracking, no personal data in URLs or logs, and clear controls for users.

ul: Consent first: load analytics and ad scripts only after opt-in where required, and make “reject” as easy as “accept”.
Keep PII out of URLs: URLs end up in logs, analytics and Referer headers.
Scrub logs and error reports: mask emails, tokens and form values before they leave the browser.
Short retention for anything you keep client-side; clear it on logout.
Payment pages: PCI DSS 4.0 asks you to inventory and justify every script on them and detect unauthorised changes, which CSP and SRI help with.

items.label: Leak less
items.sub: No PII in URLs, logs or analytics
